slides.texte_overlay:
How to stop feeling awkward
at networking events
(and actually enjoy them)
Arrive early, not fashionably late. When the room is half empty, people stand alone and are glad someone talks to them. Walking into a packed room full of closed circles is much harder.
Stand near the food or the bar. That's where people move and pause. "Have you tried these yet?" is the easiest opener in the building, and nobody finds it strange.
Join groups of three, not pairs. Two people talking might be deep in something private. A group of three is usually open. Stand at the edge, smile, and wait for a natural pause.
Swap the job question for a better one. Instead of "What do you do?", try "What are you working on that you're excited about?" People light up, and the chat feels human, not like a sales pitch.
Give yourself a small goal. Three real conversations, then you can leave. A clear finish line turns a scary evening into a short mission you can actually complete.
Try this for 30 days: five minutes a day of history, art or science. You'll always have something interesting to say that has nothing to do with your job title.
slides.texte_sophia: Try this for 30 days: five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. You'll always have something to say beyond your job title.

slides.texte_overlay: Follow up the next day. "Great meeting you last night, here's that article I mentioned." One short message turns a business card into a real contact who remembers you.
